title: Master Yuanyin on Contemplating the Mind
excerpt: The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: “The single practice of contemplating the mind encompasses all practices — it is the most essential and direct.”

inline.s: The Patriarch Bodhidharma said: “The single practice of contemplating the mind encompasses all practices — it is the most essential and direct.”

1. After we who study the Buddha’s teachings and cultivate the Way have recognized our intrinsic nature, we establish right view. Having seen the nature, originally there is nothing to cultivate, nothing to attain, and nothing to realize. Yet because your habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, when you meet with circumstances your mind is still moved — and so birth-and-death is not ended, and you must still cultivate. Why do I say so? Because after you have become a Buddha, even the Buddha is not to be attained. What thing is there left to attain? Therefore there is nothing to attain. Since there is nothing attained, what is there for you to realize? Therefore there is nothing to realize. With nothing attained and nothing realized, you are originally Buddha, not made so by practice — therefore there is nothing to cultivate. But so long as your habitual tendencies are not exhausted, you must still cultivate. How do you cultivate? The practice of non-practice is simply to contemplate and illuminate at all times, without employing any particular method to cultivate. Hence this practice of non-practice is still necessary.

2. To contemplate the mind after rising from the seat is to focus the power of the concentrated mind and watch the state before a single thought has arisen. The moment an errant thought is born, you immediately become aware of it and dispel it. Just keep watching. After a long time, the right thought that watches and the errant thought that is watched dissolve together, and then you see your original face directly. Because this method is easy to accomplish, only those replete in wholesome roots and merit are able to take it up.

3. Contemplating the mind is to watch the source where thoughts arise with vigilant awareness. When a thought comes, ask it where it comes from; when the thought subsides, ask it where it goes. To contemplate the mind is to contemplate and illuminate — to observe it and hold it in the light — so that thoughts do not rise and cease at random and flow on without rest. If you do not contemplate and illuminate, deluded thoughts fly about in profusion and your reflections multiply beyond count; instead you grow accustomed to it and no longer feel the disorder. How can that be? So you must be vigilant and watch it well. You must be clear about the true mind and the deluded mind. The mind that contemplates and illuminates is still the deluded mind, for this too is the stirring of thought. Without the true mind this deluded mind could not arise; it is what the true mind gives rise to, and it is the wondrous function of the true mind. At the very moment of its functioning — the very moment of true contemplation — do not distinguish whether it is the true mind or the deluded mind. When you have practiced until the deluded mind is unmoved, the mind that observes and the thought that is observed fall away at once — this is what is meant by “subject and object both extinguished” — and neither the observing mind nor the observed thought remains. If you do not contemplate and illuminate, there will be no extinguishing of subject and object and no breaking free; therefore you must surely contemplate and illuminate
Contemplating the mind is not watching the fleshly heart, but watching the mind-thoughts.

We who practice the Mind-Core method also contemplate the mind. While seated, we hold the mantra and listen with the mind — each syllable recited clearly, each sound heard distinctly. After rising, we contemplate and illuminate, keeping watch over the source where thoughts arise, like a cat stalking a mouse. The moment a thought arises we see it, never turning with the thought, never moved by circumstances. Now I present two methods of practice. One is: upon hearing the teaching and recognizing your intrinsic nature, you protect it at every moment — morning in this, evening in this, wandering in this, distressed in this — protecting it without movement at all times, and when a thought arises, turn it back without following it, persisting in this way for a long time. The other is to practice a specific method: either recite the Buddha’s name, or investigate Chan, or practice the Mind-Core method. Not only do you work while seated, but also after rising; you must contemplate and illuminate at all times and guard it with unbroken attentiveness — only then will it be effective.

4. Why must we contemplate and illuminate at all times? Because our thoughts are beyond counting — in a single instant there are so many thoughts. Because there are too many seeds stored in the field of the eighth consciousness; both the good and the bad are hidden within it. For example, when we look at a banana and use only the eye-consciousness rather than the thinking consciousness, the banana is simply a banana. The eye is like a camera. But if we use the thinking consciousness, then upon seeing the banana we think: “This is a banana. How delicious it is. This one is big, that one is small.” Thus the moment we use the thinking consciousness, a discriminating mind arises. The ear is the same. The thinking consciousness runs after things; the information of the six consciousnesses is handed to the seventh consciousness, which passes it to the eighth, and so seeds are created. Therefore we must contemplate and illuminate at all times. To contemplate and illuminate means: the moment a thought stirs you are aware of it, you pay it no attention, and you watch the source from which the thought arises.

5. Yesterday someone asked me about investigating Chan. He said he likes to investigate Chan and to probe “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?”, but always could not raise the sensation of doubt. I told him: to investigate Chan you must raise the sensation of doubt; if you cannot raise the sensation of doubt, it is hopeless. Better to change the method — when a thought comes, ask it where it comes from; this is not paying attention to the thought, but pursuing its origin to the very end. When the thought subsides, ask it where it goes; this is not holding onto the thought, but watching where it is extinguished. It is like a cat catching a mouse: the cat crouches at the mouse’s hole, and the moment the mouse pokes out its head, the cat leaps upon it. The mouse stands for the errant thought; you are ever vigilant like the cat, and the moment the errant thought shows its head, you immediately trace it to its origin. When the errant thought subsides, you watch where it is extinguished. This is the method of investigating Chan, whose aim, likewise, is to make “thoughts have no continuity.” Practicing this way over a long time, you turn the continuity of thoughts from familiar to unfamiliar, and the non-continuity of thoughts from unfamiliar to familiar. When the practice matures and you meet an occasion, the observing mind and the observed thought dissolve into formlessness in a single instant — with a sudden “Hu!” sound, subject and object both extinguished, the roots and the dusts fall away, and you realize the great Way.

6. After rising from the seat you should contemplate and illuminate at all times. This is harder, because people always run after circumstances. Just after rising there is still a state of concentration, and you know to watch yourself and not move about heedlessly. But once you become involved in affairs and caught up in them, you forget to contemplate and follow after circumstances, as disordered as when you were not meditating at all — this is no good. Therefore, while seated, devote yourself wholeheartedly to holding the mantra and listening with the mind; after rising, contemplate and illuminate with unbroken attentiveness, and never forget. Yet in the midst of circumstances it is easy to forget. Chat with a few friends, take up some task, and at once you are thrown into confusion. When a thought comes, pull it back quickly and watch over yourself. You must make this effort, or you will never get onto the path.

7. In contemplating the mind, the most important thing is that you always watch the source where thoughts arise — that is, focus the power of the concentrated mind and watch the state before a single thought is born. The moment a thought arises, you see it and do not run after it. When the thought is still, you watch its stillness, watching like a cat stalking a mouse. The cat stands for right thought; the mouse stands for the errant thought. The mouse hides in its hole — that is the time when the errant thought does not arise — and at such a time the cat must keep watch and not walk away. To watch this mind is itself right thought. This right thought must not be absent, for if right thought is absent, you fall into blank indifference. So you must maintain this watching of right thought. You must focus the power of the concentrated mind and watch the state before a single thought is born — that is, always watch the source where thoughts arise, and whether thoughts rise or cease, pay them no attention. Keep watching, watching; over a long, long time, suddenly it ripens and it detaches — the mind that watches and the thought that is watched both fall away. Then it is a genuine falling away: subject and object both extinguished, the fundamental opens, and you directly see your intrinsic nature.

8. Contemplating the mind is to watch the source where thoughts arise with vigilant awareness. When a thought comes, ask it where it comes from; when the thought subsides, ask it where it goes. To contemplate the mind is to contemplate and illuminate — to observe it and hold it in the light — so that thoughts do not rise and cease at random and flow on without rest. If you do not contemplate and illuminate, deluded thoughts fly about in profusion and your reflections multiply beyond count; instead you grow accustomed to it and no longer feel the disorder. How can that be? So you must be vigilant and watch it well. You must be clear about the true mind and the deluded mind. The mind that contemplates and illuminates is still the deluded mind, for this too is the stirring of thought. Without the true mind this deluded mind could not arise; it is what the true mind gives rise to, and it is the wondrous function of the true mind. At the very moment of its functioning — the very moment of true contemplation — do not distinguish whether it is the true mind or the deluded mind. When you have practiced until the deluded mind is unmoved, the mind that observes and the thought that is observed fall away at once — this is what is meant by “subject and object both extinguished,” and neither the observing mind nor the observed thought remains. If you do not contemplate and illuminate, there will be no extinguishing of subject and object and no breaking free; therefore you must surely contemplate and illuminate. Reciting the Buddha’s name is also contemplation and illumination, also cessation and insight — “Amitabha Buddha, Amitabha Buddha

, the practitioner’s thoughts are held fast by the Buddha-name; his thoughts no longer move, and this is cessation. He recites himself and listens himself, hearing each sound distinctly — this is insight. Even without voicing it aloud, when he recites Amitabha Buddha in thought he still hears it clearly — this is illumination. Guarding the Buddha-name without mixing in other thoughts is cessation; seeing the Buddha-name clearly and distinctly is insight. Contemplating the mind is not watching the fleshly heart, but watching the mind-thoughts. We who practice the Mind-Core method also contemplate the mind. While seated we hold the mantra and listen with the mind, each syllable recited clearly, each sound heard distinctly. After rising we contemplate and illuminate, keeping watch over the source of thoughts like a cat stalking a mouse. The moment a thought arises we see it, never turning with the thought, never moved by circumstances. To know the thought the instant it arises is what the Chan school calls “recognizing it” — and once recognized, one is no longer wronged!

9. If you observe only the circumstances and not the mind, you will flow along with thoughts. (For errant thoughts, even when there are no circumstances to face them, still flow on without ceasing — hence the saying “the thief within one’s own house is hard to guard against”; it is not that when no circumstance is present a single thought does not arise.) This is still useless; you must illuminate both together. The mind that contemplates and illuminates is still the deluded mind, for this too is the stirring of thought. Without the true mind this deluded mind could not arise; it is what the true mind gives rise to, and it is the wondrous function of the true mind. At the very moment of its functioning — the very moment of true contemplation — do not distinguish whether it is the true mind or the deluded mind. When you have practiced until the deluded mind is unmoved, the mind that observes and the thought that is observed fall away at once — this is what is meant by “subject and object both extinguished,” and neither the observing mind nor the observed thought remains. If you do not contemplate and illuminate, there will be no extinguishing of subject and object and no breaking free; therefore you must surely contemplate and illuminate.
10. Master Yuanyin’s discourse at Haikou
A disciple asked: “Please, Master, expound the essentials of the practice of contemplating the mind.”

Master Yuanyin answered: “In contemplating the mind, the most important thing is that you always watch the source where thoughts arise — that is, focus the power of the concentrated mind and watch the state before a single thought is born. The moment a thought arises, you see it and do not run after it. When the thought is still, you watch its stillness, watching like a cat stalking a mouse.”
A disciple asked: “What do the cat and the mouse signify as a metaphor?”

The master answered: “The cat stands for right thought, and the mouse for the errant thought. The mouse hides in its hole — that is the time when the errant thought does not arise; at such a time the cat must keep watch and not walk away. To watch this mind is right thought. This right thought must not be absent, for if right thought is absent, you fall into blank indifference.”
A disciple said: “Oh! When right thought is absent, it is blank indifference.”

The master answered: “Right! When right thought is absent, it is blank indifference. Therefore this ‘watching’ of right thought must surely be present. You must focus the power of the concentrated mind and watch the state before a single thought is born — that is, always watch the source where thoughts arise, and whether thoughts arise or cease, pay them no attention. Watch, watch; over a long, long time, suddenly it ripens and it detaches — the mind that watches and the thought that is watched both fall away. Then it is a genuine falling away: subject and object both extinguished, the fundamental opens, and you directly see your intrinsic nature.”
A disciple asked: “While contemplating the mind, if I watch too tightly, what should I do?”

The master replied: “Do not be afraid. In the past, when Masters Laiguo and Xuyun were investigating their huatou, they would often hold a bowl of rice yet forget to eat — so tightly did they hold it, so deeply were they attached. When the patrolling monk discovered them thus,
Smack!

he slapped him across the back. The Chan practitioner was startled — Oh! He has knocked away my huatou! The man was right in the midst of investigating his huatou, and had not yet reached the perfect point; the warmth of his effort was still short of the mark, when this blow startled him. Therefore, when sitting in meditation, one must not strike people in this way. When you investigate the huatou, and you have watched to exactly the right point, if from outside there comes a sound,
Whoosh!

it stirs him and he breaks open. (Note: nowadays those who practice with diligence are few, while the negligent and listless are many. How many have we seen who watched too tightly — much less need we ask about watching too tightly!)

Of course, in practice you must be good at adjusting, with a balance of tension and ease. Like the string of a lute: too loose and it goes off pitch, and can even make no sound at all; too tight and the string will break. Only with tension and ease in balance can you produce a beautiful melody. My teacher, the Venerable Xianglu, once said that practicing is like holding a bird in your hand — hold it too tightly and the bird dies, hold it too loosely and it flies away. You must neither crush the bird nor let it fly away — keep the balance of tension and ease. Practicing too tensely is also no good. For example, if in meditation you ignore the actual condition of your body and add hours and extra sessions, pressing too hard, the body cannot bear it and you will fall ill. If your body can bear it, add sessions and hours; if it cannot, ease up — in short, proceed from what is practical. In our practice, whether we are seated cultivating the method or after rising contemplating and illuminating, we must be good at harmonizing.
A disciple asked: “Master, when I contemplate the mind and see a thought come, I make it stop. Sometimes when it stops, there is no thought at all. At such a time, how should I practice?”
The master answered: “Just watch it! When there is no thought at all, just watch it!”
A disciple asked: “Watch that which has no thought?”
The master answered: “Right! The mind that watches cannot be absent, so you must watch it. Keep watching until your practice has truly reached its fulfillment,
Hu!” it breaks open, and the mind that watches is gone — then all is well.”
A disciple asked: “Master, when I contemplate the mind I often lose my hold of it. What should I do?”
The master laughed kindly: “Ha ha”
Once you forget, just pull it right back.
A disciple said: “At night when I get into bed, I merely contemplate for a moment and fall asleep.”
The master laughed kindly: “Ha ha”
You see that a thought does not stir, and you fall asleep, do you?
A disciple said: “Before, sitting in the car on the way to work, I could not fall asleep; but now the moment I contemplate the mind I fall asleep.”
The master laughed all the more warmly: “Ha ha”

This is a defect! Those who practice have two defects: one is agitation, and the other is torpor. When agitated, there are many thoughts; when thoughts are few, you fall into torpor and sleep. When you grow drowsy in practice, open your eyes — either recite the Buddha’s name or hold the mantra, and recite aloud, to drive the drowsiness away.
11. What is “Turning the Light Back” — from a recording of the Elder’s discourse at Jinan

Turning the light back — did we not just speak of it? To attend at every moment to the huatou is turning the light back. What is meant by turning the light back? It is to stop looking outward and look inward. Look at what? Look at the source where thoughts arise. The moment a thought arises, you see it and do not run after it. It is not about watching some particular place — ah. Did I not just say this: do not fixate on a point, do not fasten on some vital center, do not guard a gate. Do not dwell on any one point. Very relaxed, when a thought arises — eh, a thought has come; I pay you no attention — this is called turning the light back. At this time do not look outward, asking “what is this, what is that” — that is grasping at forms, ah. To see yet not see: as for the things outside, you see yet see nothing; though you see, you have not seen anything. The moment a thought arises I see it — I see my own thought — this is called turning the light. Contemplation and illumination is not looking outward; you must look inward. Look at what? Look at the source where thoughts arise. It is not looking at your head, not looking at your mind — no; look at the source where thoughts arise. Then you simply feel, hm, a thought has arisen. The meaning of this is: let the thought that looks outward come to rest — this is called turning the light back. It is not about looking somewhere! Not looking at my head, not looking at my mind, not looking at my dantian — none of these, none at all. Very relaxed and at ease, the moment a thought arises you know it and do not run after the thought — this is called turning the light back, ah. When a circumstance comes, do not run after it; pull yourself back — this too is called turning the light back. When a circumstance arrives, do not follow it; pull back, pull back — this is called turning the light back. If you do not know how to pull the mind back, but let it go, then the further you let it go the further it runs — that is not good. At all times you must attend to contemplation and illumination. In all four postures — walking, standing, sitting, and lying — you must contemplate and illuminate.
